strengths: The paper presents a clear and technically sound reduction of MaxSim multi-vector retrieval to learned single-vector MIPS: modeling per-token MaxSim contributions with a small MLP, pooling hidden features over query tokens, and interpreting the output-layer rows as document vectors is simple, elegant, and well motivated.

The empirical evaluation is broad and relevant. The authors compare against strong recent multi-vector retrieval systems (MUVERA, DESSERT, IGP, PLAID) on six BEIR datasets, several modern multi-vector text encoders, and two visual document retrieval models. The reported gains are large, often 5-11x QPS at 80% recall on ColBERTv2 datasets, with especially strong results on non-ColBERT embeddings.

The ablations are useful: the paper studies latent dimensionality, candidate recall versus MUVERA fixed-dimensional encodings, and the effect of approximate rather than exact MIPS. These support the central claim that learned representations can be much lower-dimensional and more accurate than data-oblivious FDEs.
The presentation is generally strong. The method is easy to follow, the mathematical formulation is concise, and the figures communicate the retrieval pipeline and speed-recall tradeoffs effectively.

The work is significant for retrieval systems: if reproduced, it offers a practical path for deploying late-interaction retrievers using standard ANNS infrastructure while retaining exact MaxSim reranking over candidates.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet fully satisfactory. The manuscript states that the code is available, but the URL is blank in the rendered PDF. The experiments also depend on several implementation choices (Glass settings, reranking implementation, embeddings, preprocessing, sampled training tokens, OLS computation) that would be difficult to reproduce exactly without released code and scripts.

The evaluation focuses almost entirely on search recall with respect to exact MaxSim neighbors and QPS. This is appropriate for an indexing paper, but the paper would be stronger with downstream retrieval-quality curves such as nDCG/Recall@k versus latency, since approximate MaxSim recall does not always translate linearly to task-level IR effectiveness.

Training and indexing costs are only partially characterized. The paper reports processing over 1000 documents/s for OLS-style indexing, but does not provide complete build-time, training-time, index-size, memory, or update-cost tables across datasets and baselines. This matters because LEMUR learns corpus-specific document vectors and still needs multi-vector representations for reranking.

The fairness of baseline tuning is somewhat hard to assess. LEMUR and MUVERA use the same Glass backend, while DESSERT, IGP, and PLAID use their official implementations with mostly recommended index hyperparameters and limited extra tuning. More detailed tuning budgets and memory-normalized comparisons would make the claimed dominance more convincing.

The limitations section is honest but narrow. It mainly discusses compatibility with compression and does not deeply analyze failure modes such as query-distribution shift, dynamic corpora, very small training samples, multilingual/domain shift behavior, or cases where learned document-specific output weights might overfit corpus-specific MaxSim structure.

The paper does not discuss research ethics or broader impacts. The topic has limited direct ethical risk, but retrieval systems can affect access to information and may inherit biases from embedding models and corpora; a brief discussion would be appropriate.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in multi-vector retrieval: the latency cost of exact MaxSim search. Reducing candidate generation to single-vector MIPS while preserving exact MaxSim reranking is a useful and practically relevant direction.

The core construction is simple and reasonably well motivated: learn a token-level function approximating each document's MaxSim contribution, then interpret the linear output weights and pooled hidden activations as document/query vectors in a latent space.

The empirical coverage is broader than many systems papers in this area: experiments include six BEIR datasets, several modern multi-vector text encoders, and visual document retrieval models, rather than only ColBERTv2.

The reported speedups are large and consistent across settings. Table 2 and Figures 4-6 indicate substantial QPS gains over MUVERA, PLAID, DESSERT, and IGP at comparable recall, including on large corpora such as MS MARCO and HotpotQA.

The ablations on latent dimension, candidate set recall, ANN vs exact latent search, and training-query distribution help explain several implementation choices and suggest the method is not overly fragile to one specific training-data construction.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too latency-centric and omits key systems costs. The method learns a 2048-dimensional vector per document; for millions of documents this is a very large additional index, yet memory footprint, index size, training time, build time, and update costs are not reported in the main comparison. This makes the practical superiority claim incomplete.

Reproducibility is weaker than it should be. The manuscript says the code is available, but the URL appears blank in the provided text. Several implementation details that materially affect performance, such as exact Glass settings beyond R/L, scalar quantization configuration, reranking implementation details, and full hyperparameter grids, are only partially specified.

The fairness of the baseline comparison is not fully convincing. LEMUR is paired with a strong modern HNSW implementation and custom C++ reranking; some baselines use official implementations or fast-plaid with mostly fixed recommended hyperparameters. The paper does not provide enough evidence that each baseline is tuned to its best memory/latency/recall tradeoff under the same constraints.

The method is corpus-specific and transductive: document representations are output-layer weights fitted against a fixed corpus. This is a meaningful limitation for dynamic collections, but the paper treats indexing new documents briefly and does not quantify incremental insertion quality, retraining needs, or distribution shift effects.

The central retrieval metric is recall with respect to exact MaxSim nearest neighbors, not downstream IR effectiveness. Exact MaxSim reranking preserves quality only if the candidate set has sufficient recall, but the paper does not show end-to-end nDCG/MRR degradation or user-facing retrieval quality under realistic latency budgets.

The theoretical discussion is limited. The supervised reduction is intuitive, but there are no approximation guarantees, no analysis of when the learned latent inner product should preserve MaxSim rankings, and little discussion of failure modes for different embedding distributions or long visual documents.

The limitations section is too narrow. It mentions multi-vector storage and low-precision compression, but does not seriously address the added learned-index memory, training/build costs, dynamic corpora, baseline tuning ambiguity, or possible data/query leakage concerns from using corpus documents encoded as pseudo-queries.

Presentation is generally clear, but some important empirical details are relegated to figures without numerical tables, and the claimed 'order of magnitude faster' result depends on selected recall operating points rather than a comprehensive resource-normalized comparison.

strengths: The paper proposes a clean and useful reduction of MaxSim multi-vector retrieval to single-vector MIPS by learning a low-dimensional latent representation whose inner products approximate per-document MaxSim scores. The formulation is simple, technically sound, and likely easy to integrate with existing ANN infrastructure.

The empirical evaluation is broad and convincing: results cover six BEIR datasets with ColBERTv2, four additional modern multi-vector text models, and two visual document retrieval models on ViDoRe. LEMUR consistently improves the QPS-recall tradeoff, with especially large gains over MUVERA, PLAID, DESSERT, and IGP on several non-ColBERTv2 embeddings.

The paper includes useful ablations on latent dimension, exact versus approximate latent-space search, and training-set choice. These studies support the main design decisions and show robustness to using corpus-derived pseudo-query data when real training queries are unavailable.

Presentation is generally clear. The method is explained with a concise decomposition from token-level target function to pooled latent query representation and learned document weights, and the experimental protocol is described in enough detail to understand the comparisons.

Reproducibility is reasonably strong: the manuscript reports model-training hyperparameters, ANN settings, baseline implementations, datasets, hardware, and query/index hyperparameter search procedures, and states that code will be released.
weaknesses: The paper focuses almost entirely on speed and recall with respect to exact MaxSim nearest neighbors, but it does not show downstream retrieval effectiveness metrics such as nDCG, MRR, or Recall@k against relevance judgments after approximate search. This is mostly acceptable for a similarity-search paper, but it would strengthen the practical claim that the speedups preserve end-task quality.

Memory and indexing costs are underdeveloped. LEMUR adds learned 2048-dimensional document vectors plus the original multi-vector representations for reranking; the paper discusses latency but does not provide a full memory/index-build/training-time comparison against baselines, which is important for large-scale retrieval deployment.

The fairness of baseline tuning is mostly reasonable but not fully airtight. Some baselines use recommended fixed index hyperparameters while DESSERT receives a small grid search; it is not clear whether all methods are equally optimized for each embedding family and dataset, especially given the strong claims about baseline failures on newer models.

The limitations section is brief. It mentions memory compression and low-precision compatibility, but does not deeply discuss possible failure modes from distribution shift between corpus-derived training tokens and real queries, sensitivity to corpus updates, or scaling behavior when the number of documents becomes much larger.

The method is elegant but not theoretically characterized: there are no approximation guarantees or analysis of when the learned latent regression should preserve MaxSim rankings. The strong empirical evidence largely compensates, but the contribution is more empirical/systems-oriented than foundational.

strengths: The paper proposes a clean and technically plausible reduction of MaxSim multi-vector search to learned single-vector MIPS: train a shallow multi-output regressor for token-to-document MaxSim contributions, interpret the linear output weights as document vectors, and retrieve candidates with an ANN index before exact MaxSim reranking. The derivation is simple, well presented, and matches the implementation.

The empirical evaluation is broad and relevant: 8 BEIR datasets, ColBERTv2 plus several newer multi-vector text models, and two visual-document models on ViDoRe. The reported end-to-end speedups over MUVERA, PLAID, DESSERT, and IGP are large and consistent, including 5-16x better QPS at >=80% recall on ColBERTv2 datasets.

The paper includes useful ablations and diagnostics: latent dimension, candidate recall, MaxSim correlation, long queries, training-data selection, and random hidden-layer features. These make the central mechanism more convincing than a black-box speed benchmark alone.

The method is practically attractive because it leverages standard single-vector ANN infrastructure and appears easy to integrate with existing HNSW-like systems. The indexing pipeline and hyperparameters are described clearly enough to understand the computational steps.

Presentation is strong overall. The motivation, algorithms, figures, and limitations are easy to follow, and the paper situates the work well relative to token-pruning systems and MUVERA-style fixed-dimensional encodings.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is weaker than expected for a systems-heavy empirical paper. The abstract says code is available but the URL is missing, and the paper relies on several implementation choices, custom C++ reranking, Glass settings, and large precomputed embeddings that are not packaged or described at a level that would make independent replication straightforward.

Memory usage is a major missing evaluation dimension. LEMUR stores learned 2048-dimensional document vectors, an ANN graph, and still needs original multi-vector document embeddings for reranking. The paper claims lower memory than MUVERA and discusses storage qualitatively, but does not report index size, RAM during querying, or memory-latency tradeoffs across methods.

The fairness of baseline tuning is not fully convincing. The paper uses recommended hyperparameters for most baselines and performs a grid search only for DESSERT, while LEMUR benefits from a modern HNSW implementation and scalar quantization. More systematic tuning or sensitivity analysis for all methods would strengthen the speedup claims.

The theoretical result is mostly a universal-approximation sanity check and does not explain the finite-sample behavior, ranking preservation, or why small sampled OLS targets suffice at corpus scale. The strong empirical results carry the paper, but the theory provides limited assurance beyond representability.

The method is corpus-specific and requires training/index recomputation steps whose operational implications are only partially explored. Incremental indexing, drift, cross-corpus reuse, and updates are discussed briefly but not evaluated in realistic dynamic settings.

The impact statement is too cursory. Retrieval infrastructure can affect access to information, ranking biases, and deployment energy/cost; even if the work is primarily technical, dismissing direct societal impact leaves ethics and downstream risks underexamined.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in multi-vector retrieval: reducing MaxSim retrieval latency while preserving recall. This is a significant problem for ColBERT-style and visual document retrieval systems.

The main construction is simple and technically coherent: learn a feature map for per-token support-function values, pool query-token features, and interpret the output-layer rows as document vectors for MIPS followed by exact MaxSim reranking.

The empirical section is broader than many papers in this area, covering eight BEIR datasets, several modern multi-vector text encoders, and two visual document retrieval encoders. The reported CPU speedups over MUVERA, PLAID, DESSERT, and IGP are substantial, especially at 80% recall.

Presentation is generally clear. The method, indexing/query algorithms, and hyperparameters are easy to follow, and the limitations section acknowledges memory compression and incremental-indexing challenges.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not yet reproducible enough for acceptance. The abstract says code is available but gives no URL, and the paper relies on several implementation choices (Glass/HNSW settings, C++ reranking, PyTorch inference, scalar quantization, baseline wrappers) that materially affect latency.

The comparison is potentially under-specified and may be unfair. LEMUR and MUVERA are integrated into Glass with the same reranker, while other baselines use their own implementations and mostly recommended/default index parameters. Only DESSERT receives an explicit grid search. This makes the large QPS gaps hard to attribute cleanly to the proposed representation rather than implementation/tuning differences.

The theoretical contribution is weak. The universal-approximation result is essentially vacuous for this setting: it establishes existence of a sufficiently large MLP for a fixed compact domain, but gives no sample complexity, dimension requirement, ranking-preservation guarantee, or explanation of when the learned MIPS reduction should work at useful recall.

The method is corpus-specific and requires storing both the learned single-vector index and the original multi-vector document representations for reranking, but memory footprint is not reported in a comparable way. This is a major omission because memory is one of the central constraints in multi-vector retrieval.

The evaluation emphasizes recall relative to exact MaxSim neighbors, with only limited nDCG preservation checks. It does not sufficiently analyze user-facing retrieval quality tradeoffs across the newer text and visual models, nor the effect of missed candidates on final task metrics.

Some operational claims are under-supported. The paper states that new documents can be indexed quickly by solving linear regression and inserting into HNSW, but gives no dynamic-update experiments, degradation measurements, or costs for repeated incremental updates.

The limitations and ethics discussion is thin. The statement that the work has no direct societal impact is too dismissive for retrieval infrastructure that may affect access to information, ranking bias, and downstream RAG systems. This is not a fatal issue, but it weakens the paper’s treatment of broader impacts.

Originality is moderate rather than strong. Recasting MaxSim approximation as supervised regression followed by a learned single-vector reduction is useful, but it is close in spirit to distillation/random-feature/kernel-approximation ideas and corpus-specific indexing. The paper would need stronger analysis or more airtight benchmarking to justify the strength of its claims.

strengths: The paper presents a simple and compelling reduction of MaxSim multi-vector retrieval to learned single-vector MIPS: train a shallow model to approximate per-token MaxSim contributions, interpret the output weights as document vectors, retrieve with a standard ANNS index, then rerank exactly. The formulation is clean and practically appealing.

The empirical evaluation is broad and relevant: eight BEIR datasets, several modern multi-vector text models, two visual document retrieval models, and comparisons to PLAID, DESSERT, IGP, and MUVERA. The reported speedups are large and consistent, including 5-16x higher QPS than the best baseline at >=80% recall on ColBERTv2 embeddings.

The work includes useful ablations on latent dimension, candidate set size, long queries, training-set source, and random hidden features. These help support the claim that the method is robust and that the learned latent representation is substantially more efficient than MUVERA-style fixed-dimensional encodings.

The implementation story is practical: the method uses a small MLP, OLS for final document weights, an off-the-shelf HNSW implementation, and exact reranking. The authors also report indexing/training time on the largest dataset and discuss incremental updates.

The paper is clearly written, well motivated, and positioned against prior multi-vector search systems. The limitations section is honest about memory compression and operational issues in incremental indexing.
weaknesses: The theoretical analysis is quite weak relative to the strength of the empirical claims. The universal approximation argument is essentially generic and does not provide finite-sample, ranking, top-k recall, or distributional guarantees; it mainly justifies representability in principle.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the submitted manuscript: the abstract says code is available but the URL appears blank. Hyperparameters are listed, but the missing repository link and reliance on multiple specialized baseline implementations make independent reproduction harder.

The evaluation emphasizes MaxSim recall/QPS, while downstream retrieval quality is only checked via nDCG@10 for ColBERTv2 on BEIR. Similar downstream quality checks for the newer text models and visual models would strengthen the claim that the approximation preserves task performance beyond nearest-neighbor recall.

The comparison would benefit from more explicit memory accounting. The paper argues that lower-dimensional learned vectors reduce memory and latency, but does not present a full memory breakdown including learned weights, original multi-vector storage for reranking, ANNS index overhead, and baseline indexes.

Baseline tuning may not be fully balanced. The authors mostly use recommended hyperparameters and grid-search DESSERT, but stronger tuning or sensitivity analysis for all baselines would make the large performance gaps more convincing, especially since these systems can be sensitive to clustering, probing, and reranking settings.

The method is corpus-specific and requires training plus OLS over documents before indexing. The largest reported setup takes 4.8 hours on CPU, which is reasonable, but the paper does not deeply evaluate dynamic corpora, deletion/update costs, or distribution shift as the corpus evolves.
